title: It Takes a Team to Break a Record
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Admired Leadership uses Sabastian Sawe's sub-two-hour marathon in London (1:59:30) as a vehicle for arguing that peak performance in any domain is now a systems achievement rather than an individual one. What appears to be a solitary athletic achievement is the product of 5-10 specialists in physiology, biomechanics, nutrition, psychology, logistics, data science, and technology—a Formula 1 pit crew model applied to individual sport. The article draws a direct parallel to organizational leadership: the 'hero leader' model is obsolete, replaced by performance ecosystems that include executive coaches, chiefs of staff, strategic advisors, technology specialists, peer advisory networks, and wellness experts. The central leadership question has shifted from 'How exceptional is the leader?' to 'How well designed is the system supporting this leader's judgment, energy, and execution?'—a reframe from talent identification to environment design. Leaders who can integrate human judgment with data and machine intelligence have marked advantage, but this integration itself requires a team and the orchestration of expertise across domains.
points: What looks like solitary achievement—a marathon record, an exemplary leadership decision—is actually the product of a carefully assembled performance ecosystem; modern records are collaborative systems achievements.
The 'hero leader' model is officially obsolete: organizations are building support ecosystems around their best leaders, shifting the design question from individual excellence to system quality.

The key question is now 'How well designed is the system supporting this leader?'—a structural reframe that moves from talent identification to environment design as the primary leadership investment.

Marginal gains philosophy applies directly to leadership: small improvements across a well-designed support system produce large performance differences when competition is tight, where isolated individual brilliance cannot.

The leader's role shifts from having all the answers to orchestrating expertise—integrating human judgment with data and machine intelligence across a team of specialists who extend the leader's effective range.
quotes: In today's world, peak performance emerges as much from the quality of support and coordination of a team of experts as from the raw talent and individual training of the performers. Athletes, and corporate athletes alike, depend on teams of support people to excel.

The old model was a single coach, a single training program, plus hard work. The modern formula resembles a Formula 1 pit crew. From strength specialists to recovery experts, athletes draw on many disciplines to rework their training and approach to competition.
Setting new records is a team achievement, not an individual success story. Small changes make for big differences when the competition is fierce. It now takes a team of people to create an edge.

The question has shifted from 'How exceptional is the leader?' to 'How well designed is the system supporting this leader's judgment, energy, and execution?' Just as athletes use biometrics and video analysis, leaders are increasingly turning to behavior analytics, scenario planning, cognitive performance tools, and AI-assisted modeling.

The leader's role becomes less about having all the answers and more about orchestrating expertise. Leaders who can integrate human judgment with data and machine intelligence have a marked advantage. This takes a team of experts, not isolated brilliance.
